Q22_6_TEXT: These issues cannot really be separated. Preschool expansion removes three- and four-year-olds from private child care centers, which changes the financial model that allows us to serve children from birth through age five. Infant and toddler care requires significantly more staff per child and is the most expensive care we provide. Preschool enrollment helps offset those higher costs. When that enrollment moves to publicly funded programs, our fixed costs do not go away. We are left with a greater concentration of the most expensive children to serve and less revenue to support the overall program.  At the same time, we are expected to compete for qualified teachers with public programs that can offer higher salaries, health insurance, retirement benefits, paid time off, and other benefits that small child care businesses simply cannot match. We cannot solve that disparity by continually increasing tuition because families cannot afford what it would actually cost to fund comparable compensation, particularly in infant and toddler classrooms.  This creates a cycle: preschool enrollment is lost, revenue is reduced, staffing becomes harder to afford, qualified teachers leave for better compensation, and our ability to maintain enrollment and classroom capacity is further reduced.  This is not simply a problem of "low enrollment." It is a structural problem with the current funding model. If preschool expansion is going to be sustainable, New Jersey must protect the private child care infrastructure that provides infant and toddler care and make meaningful use of private providers in its mixed-delivery system. Otherwise, we are solving the preschool issue by shifting the child care crisis to children under three.

Q24_10_TEXT: Tuition increases reflect the cumulative cost of operating a licensed child care center, not one isolated expense. NJ minimum wage increases affect our entire wage scale because experienced staff must remain appropriately compensated above entry-level wages. At the same time, we are competing for qualified employees with publicly funded programs that can offer higher salaries and benefit packages that small child care businesses cannot match.  Our experience with Grow NJ Kids illustrates the larger problem. Participation required additional paid staff training and meeting time, classroom coverage while employees completed those requirements, and additional implementation resources. We ultimately had to pause participation because the cost was greater than anticipated and had to be weighed against staff compensation, hiring needs, and the overall financial viability of the center.

Q27_7_TEXT: Our primary goal for 2026–2027 is to hold on and maintain the services we currently provide. The need for infant and toddler care is greater than the number of children we are able to accommodate, yet expanding that capacity would require substantial capital investment to retrofit our existing building to meet current requirements for additional infant/toddler space.  This is an area where State investment could make a meaningful difference. If preschool expansion is reducing the private market for three- and four-year-olds while demand for infant and toddler care continues to exceed supply, funding should be available to help established licensed centers modify existing facilities so they can expand birth-to-three capacity.  The State also needs to address the workforce disparity directly. One meaningful solution would be a statewide pooled benefits program for eligible child care employees actively working and registered through NJCCIS. Access to group health insurance, retirement/401(k) participation, and educational assistance would begin to address benefits that individual small child care businesses will never have the purchasing power to provide at the same level as public employers.  If New Jersey wants private providers to maintain and expand infant and toddler capacity, investment cannot focus only on creating preschool seats. It must also address the facilities and workforce needed to care for children before they reach preschool.
